4 · One scene, six ways of saying it.

1 · Read the explanation.
Describing a scene, and checking you have been understood

Position first, then detail. English descriptions usually move from the whole to the part: in the foreground, in the background, on the left, at the top, behind him, in the middle distance. Give the position, then the object, then the adjectives.

Adjective order, from lesson 41. Opinion → size → quality → shape → age → colour → origin → material. A large black panther, brightly coloured dresses, a stiff green leaf pattern. Two or three at a time; move the rest behind the noun.

Sense verbs, from lesson 43. Can is normal with the senses: I can see, you can almost hear, I could smell. You look at a picture and watch what happens in it. After look, seem and sound, an adjective; with like, a noun.

Impressions and guesses. A photograph does not answer questions, so mark what you are inferring: they seem to be…, it looks as though…, it must be winter, it might be a market, some sort of rope.

Checking. Three different problems, three different phrases. A word you did not catch: Sorry, did you say ‘cooking’? A word you heard but do not understand: What do you mean by ‘on the water’? Your own understanding of the whole idea: Am I right in thinking that…? And when the other person is lost: You look a bit confused, Do you see what I mean?

Summarising a comparison. They are the same in that both are markets, and different in that mine… This is the sentence that ends the recording, and it is worth learning whole.

The commonest errors at this level
  • on the foreground — it is in the foreground.
  • What do you mean with…? — the preposition is by.
  • They seem be women — seem to be.
  • It looks stiffly — an adjective after look.
  • a black large panther — size before colour.

Two things to watch

1 — Say where before you say what. A reader who does not know where to look cannot use the adjectives you give them.

2 — Mark every inference. They seem to be women and they are women are different claims, and in a description of a photograph only one of them is safe.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Building one sentence of description

What you see: at the front of the painting, an animal; it is a panther; it is black; it is large; you think it is about to jump.

Step 1 — position first. In the foreground…

Step 2 — order the adjectives. Size before colour: a large black panther.

Step 3 — mark what you are guessing. You cannot know its intention, so: it looks as though it is about to pounce, or it seems ready to pounce.

Step 4 — add another sense if you can. You can almost hear the jungle behind it.

The result: In the foreground there is a large black panther, and it looks as though it is about to pounce.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Where things are, and how sure you are

Position takes fixed prepositions: in the foreground, in the background, in the middle — but on the left, on the right, and at the top, at the bottom. These are not chosen; they are learned.

What you can perceive uses can or could with the sense verb: You can almost hear the clatter · I can’t see anyone cooking. English uses can see rather than the continuous here.

Impressions: They seem to be women · It looks as though it is winter — seem and appear take to be or a clause; look takes as though or as if before a clause.

Hedging a thing you cannot name: some sort of rope · a kind of basket · something like a stove. Deduction: It must be winter — look at the boots · it can’t be summer.

Checking, which is a skill and not an admission

Three different things get checked, and each has its own phrase. One word you did not catch: Sorry, did you say ‘cooking’? — repeat the word itself. A meaning: What do you mean by ‘on the water’? — note that by is obligatory: What do you mean with. Your own understanding: Am I right in thinking they are in boats? — a full clause follows, with no inversion.

Describing an image, keep the adjective order from lesson 41 — a large black panther, size before colour — and remember that an adverb plus a participle counts as one unit and takes no hyphen: brightly coloured dresses.

The register point worth taking away: hedging and checking make you sound more competent, not less. A speaker who says it’s some sort of rope and am I right in thinking…? is managing uncertainty out loud, which is what fluent speakers do; a speaker who guesses confidently and gets it wrong has to reverse.

Errors to watch: on the foreground → in the foreground · in the left → on the left · What do you mean with that? → by that · Am I right in thinking are they in boats? → no inversion · It seems to be winter, it looks like it is — choose one structure.

Stage 5 · Speaking & WritingWriting

One scene, described so it can be drawn

The test of a description is simple: could somebody who has never seen it draw it from your words?

The brief

Choose one image you know well — a photograph, a painting, a view from a window. Describe it so precisely that a reader could reproduce it: position first, then object, then adjectives in the right order, with every guess marked as a guess and at least one sense other than sight.

1 · Make notes before you speak. One line each.
1The image, in five words:

1 · Read the model description.
Model · a scene described in four paragraphs

The painting is almost square, and at first it reads as a wall of green. Only after a few seconds do you find the two things it is actually about: an animal on the left, and a small figure in the top right corner that most people never see at all.

In the foreground there is a large black panther, standing rather than crouching, with its head turned away from us. It is impossible to tell whether it is about to pounce or has just decided not to. Around it the jungle is too orderly to be real: the same stiff leaf pattern repeats eleven times, and the leaves look as though they had been cut out of metal and painted afterwards. A length of thick brown rope hangs from the branch above the animal, which nobody has ever explained.

In the background the sky is threatening, a heavy grey-green that does not appear anywhere else in the picture. The small figure stands under it in rubber boots, which is the detail that dates the painting, and seems to be carrying something. It might be a lamp; it might be a bird. The border around the whole scene is purely decorative, and it is the only part with any red in it.

What is remarkable is how quiet it is. Every predator in the picture is looking away from the viewer, and there is no wind in the stiff leaves. You would expect to hear a clatter from somewhere and you can hear nothing, which is probably why colour-blind visitors, who see the greens as one flat tone, often describe it as the calmest thing in the room.
